title: IBM Expands Qiskit Beyond Python with Native C API Bindings for Fortran, C++, and Julia - Quantum Computing Report
gist: IBM Quantum released native C API bindings (qiskit.h) exposing Qiskit v2.0's Rust core to Fortran, C++ and Julia, so HPC simulation codes can call quantum circuits without a Python interpreter. The move targets tightly coupled quantum-centric supercomputing workflows in chemistry, physics and materials science.

themes.theme: Qiskit moves into the HPC language stack

insights.claim: IBM Quantum introduced native C API bindings (qiskit.h) connecting Qiskit v2.0's Rust data model to Fortran, C++, and Julia, the primary programming languages of high-performance computing.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: IBM is extending its quantum SDK from the Python developer funnel into the compiled-language world where supercomputing budgets and users live.

insights.claim: Classical supercomputing simulation codes in chemistry, physics, and material science rely heavily on compiled languages, which is why Python-only access limited quantum adoption in those workloads.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: The addressable user base for quantum-HPC integration is existing compiled-code scientific software, not new Python developers.
insights.quote: While Python remains the standard entry point for quantum software development, classical supercomputing simulation codes in chemistry, physics, and material science rely heavily on compiled languages.
insights.locator: While Python remains the standard entry point

insights.claim: Exposing a unified C interface to Qiskit's Rust core lets researchers build, transpile, and execute circuits inside classical HPC applications without an intermediate Python interpreter or Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) overhead.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Removing the Python layer cuts latency in the classical-quantum loop, which matters for variational and time-evolution algorithms that call hardware repeatedly.
insights.locator: By exposing a unified C interface

themes.theme: Target ecosystems named in the bindings

insights.claim: The bindings map to specific incumbent scientific software: qiskit-fortran targets GAMESS, Quantum ESPRESSO, CP2K, VASP and BIGSTICK; qiskit-cpp targets LAMMPS, GROMACS and GPU layers like CUDA and Kokkos; Qiskit.jl targets DifferentialEquations.jl and ITensors.jl.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: The named codes are the likely first integration points and a checklist of where quantum-assisted chemistry and materials pilots could appear.
insights.locator: Summary of Qiskit Native Language Bindings

insights.claim: Because all three bindings interface with the same Qiskit shared library, they are fully interoperable, so a circuit built in Fortran can be passed to a C++ execution module or a Julia post-processing pipeline without data conversion.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: A single shared core lets mixed-language HPC teams standardize on Qiskit rather than maintain separate quantum toolchains.
insights.locator: Because all three language bindings interface

insights.claim: The native bindings are aimed at tightly coupled quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) workflows such as Hamiltonian simulation, variational optimization, and Trotterized time-evolution, with circuit calls embedded as linked subroutines that keep classical memory structures and compiler optimizations.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: IBM is positioning quantum hardware as an accelerator called from inside HPC codes, analogous to GPUs, which favors vendors with strong supercomputing-center relationships.
